define-assembly.name: prop-definitions
define-assembly.description: Defines the namespaced properties that may be used in this catalog and in every document that imports it, organized by the element types on which the properties are permitted.

define-assembly.name: definition-set
define-assembly.description: The properties defined for one or more element types.

define-field.name: element
define-field.description: The name of an element type on which the properties of this set are permitted.

remarks.p: The value is the name of the Metaschema definition of the element type, not the name under which the element type is used in a given model. The two differ where one name is used for different definitions: a component in a system security plan is a system-component, while a component in a component definition is a defined-component.
Where the OSCAL models contain more than one definition with the same name, such as implemented-requirement in the system security plan and component definition models, the name covers all of them.
An element type may belong to any OSCAL model, not only to the catalog model, since the definitions of a catalog apply to the documents that import it.

define-field.name: description
define-field.description: A summary of the purpose of the properties defined for the listed element types.

define-assembly.name: prop-definition
define-assembly.description: Defines one property permitted on the listed element types: its namespace and name, its value space, its occurrence rules, and the classes of computation it modifies.

define-flag.name: name
define-flag.description: The name of the properties governed by this definition.

define-flag.name: ns
define-flag.description: The namespace of the properties governed by this definition, identifying the organization that publishes and governs the property.

remarks.p: This value must be an absolute URI that serves as a naming system identifier. It must not be the OSCAL namespace http://csrc.nist.gov/ns/oscal, whose properties are defined by the OSCAL models.

define-flag.name: label
define-flag.description: A short human-readable label for the property, suitable for naming the field in a user interface.

define-flag.name: datatype
define-flag.description: The datatype that a value of this property must conform to.

allowed-values.enum: Any string of characters; the default when no datatype is given.
A non-colonized name with no whitespace.
A boolean value: true, false, 1, or 0.
A whole number.
A decimal number.
A date with optional timezone.
A date and time with a required timezone.
An absolute URI.
A URI or a relative reference.
A version 4 or 5 universally unique identifier.

remarks.p: The names and lexical rules of these datatypes are those of the Metaschema simple datatypes already used throughout OSCAL. Value spaces needing rules beyond a datatype are expressed with pattern or allowed-value entries.

define-flag.name: required
define-flag.description: Whether every instance of the listed element types must carry this property.

allowed-values.enum: Every instance of a listed element type must carry this property at least once.
The property is optional.

define-flag.name: repeatable
define-flag.description: Whether one instance of a listed element type may carry this property more than once, expressing a list of values.

allowed-values.enum: The property may appear multiple times on one element instance; each occurrence contributes one value to a list.
The property may appear at most once on one element instance.

define-flag.name: allow-other
define-flag.description: When allowed-value entries are provided, whether values outside that enumeration are also permitted.

allowed-values.enum: The enumerated values are documented suggestions; other values conforming to the datatype and pattern are also permitted.
The value space is closed to the enumerated values.

define-flag.name: pattern
define-flag.description: An XML Schema regular expression that a value of this property must match in its entirety.

define-field.name: description
define-field.description: A summary of the property's meaning.

define-field.name: allowed-value
define-field.description: A permitted value of the property, with documentation of the value's meaning as the field's content.

define-flag.name: value
define-flag.description: The literal value permitted for the property.

define-field.name: modifies
define-field.description: Declares a class of computation whose outcome depends on understanding this property.

allowed-values.enum: The property is a legitimate basis for selecting controls (e.g., during profile import); a selection computed over content carrying this property is unreliable without understanding it.
The property alters how content may be modified (e.g., during profile tailoring and merge).
The property alters what satisfying a requirement means for assessment purposes.
The property changes the normative presentation of content; a generic rendering is not faithful without understanding it.
The property is informational only and modifies no class of computation; processing never needs to halt on account of it.

remarks.p: Each permitted value is enumerated exactly once.

expect.description: The value 'none' is an explicit declaration that no computation class is modified, and therefore cannot be combined with any other value; a definition that both modifies nothing and modifies something is contradictory and would defeat deterministic fail-closed processing.

remarks.p: The required and repeatable rules count occurrences per instance of a listed element type. Together they express four cardinalities: zero or one (the default), exactly one (required), zero or more (repeatable), and one or more (both). Repetition replaces delimiter-joined values packed into one string, which corrupt on the first value containing the delimiter.

When one or more allowed-value entries are provided, the property's value space is closed to those values unless allow-other is yes. The datatype, pattern, and allowed-value facilities compose: a conforming value must satisfy all that are present.

If no modifies value is provided, consumers must behave as if all computation classes other than none were declared. The safe default is the conservative reading: the burden of declaring a property harmless rests with its publisher, not with its consumers.

A tool performing a computation of a declared class (for example, profile resolution performing selection) over content that carries this property, without implementing the property, must halt with an error identifying the property and this definition, rather than proceed to a silently incorrect result. Tools must not modify or remove properties they do not implement.
A set lists each element type at most once.
Within a set, each property is defined exactly once; two definitions for one ns and name would make the governing value and occurrence rules ambiguous.

A catalog is the authoritative source of its controls. With this assembly it is also the authoritative source of the namespaced properties used to annotate those controls and the objects that implement or assess them. The definitions apply to the catalog itself and to every document that imports it, directly or through a chain of imports, such as a profile, a component definition, or a system security plan. A consumer of such a document obtains the definitions by resolving the import chain to the catalog. The definitions have no version of their own: their version is the version given in the catalog's metadata.

A prop is governed by a definition when the element type of its containing object is listed by the definition's set and its ns and name equal those of the definition. The combination of element type, ns, and name identifies a definition and must be unique across all sets of a catalog.

A namespace used by any definition is closed for the catalog and for the documents that import it: every prop in that namespace must be governed by a definition. A misspelled name, or a property placed on an element type for which it is not defined, is an error and not an unrecognized extension. Namespaces that no definition uses are unaffected, so existing content remains valid.

A prop may omit its ns when exactly one definition applicable to the element type of its containing object has the prop's name; the namespace of the prop is then the one given by that definition. When more than one applicable definition has that name, the ns must be provided. A definition must not use a name that the OSCAL models define in the OSCAL namespace for the same element type, so that a property without a ns never changes its meaning. Providing the ns remains valid in every case.

Constraints defined by the OSCAL models, or by an organization's Metaschema-based extension of them, take precedence over the definitions in this assembly. The definitions are a lightweight alternative for publishers and consumers that do not exchange Metaschema modules, not a replacement for them.

Generic schema validation and the constraints defined on this model check the structure of the definitions. Checking properties against the definitions (names, element types, occurrence, datatype, pattern, allowed-value conformance, the uniqueness of definitions across sets, and the resolution of an omitted ns) is performed by tools implementing this mechanism. Because the definitions are data, this check is mechanical and requires no publisher-specific code.

Profile resolution carries the definitions of the imported catalogs into the resolved catalog, as described by the profile resolution specification. Catalogs that define the same combination of element type, ns, and name differently cannot be resolved together.

remarks.p: Each security or privacy control within the catalog is defined by a distinct control instance. Controls may be as complex or as simple as a catalog defines them. They may be decomposed or further specified into child control objects, for example to represent control enhancements or specific breakouts of control functionality, to be maintained as discrete requirements. Controls may also contain structured parts (using part) and they may be grouped together in families or classes with group.

Control structures in OSCAL will also exhibit regularities and rules that are not codified in OSCAL but in its applications or domains of application. For example, for catalogs describing controls as defined by NIST SP 800-53, a control must have a part with the name "statement", which represents the textual narrative of the control. This "statement" part must occur only once, but may have nested parts to allow for multiple paragraphs or sections of text. This organization supports addressability of this data content as long as, and only insofar as, it is consistently implemented across the control set. As given with these model definitions, constraints defined and assigned here can aid in ensuring this regularity; but other such constraints and other useful patterns of use remain to be discovered and described.
